## Problem 1
Write a function that draws birthdays for a group and checks for duplicates.
```{r}
birthday_repeated = function(n_people) {

  if (!is.numeric(n_people)) {
    stop("n_people must be numeric")
  } else if (n_people < 2) {
    stop("n_people should be 2 or more")
  }

  birthdays = sample(1:365, size = n_people, replace = TRUE)

  repeated = length(unique(birthdays)) < n_people

  repeated

}
```

Run it 10000 times for each group size between 2 and 50.

```{r}
birthday_results_df =
  expand_grid(
    n_people = 2:50,
    iter = 1:10000
  ) |>
  mutate(
    repeated = map_lgl(n_people, birthday_repeated)
  ) |>
  group_by(n_people) |>
  summarize(prob_repeat = mean(repeated))
```

Plot the probability as a function of group size.

```{r}
birthday_results_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = n_people, y = prob_repeat)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line() +
  labs(
    title = "Probability of a shared birthday by group size",
    x = "Group size",
    y = "Probability of at least one shared birthday"
  )
```

```{r include = FALSE}
n_half =
  birthday_results_df |>
  filter(prob_repeat > 0.5) |>
  pull(n_people) |>
  min()

prob_50 =
  birthday_results_df |>
  filter(n_people == 50) |>
  pull(prob_repeat)
```

The probability of a shared birthday increases quickly with group size. It is close to 0 for very small groups, passes 50% at a group size of `r n_half`, and reaches about `r round(prob_50 * 100, 1)`% with 50 people. Therefore, even a moderately sized group is likely to have at least two people with the same birthday.


## Problem 2

Start with a dataframe of all file names, then read in data for each subject using map.

```{r message = FALSE}
study_df =
  tibble(
    files = list.files("data/", pattern = "\\.csv$"),
    path = str_c("data/", files)
  ) |>
  mutate(data = map(path, read_csv)) |>
  unnest(data)
```

Tidy the result: get arm and subject ID from the file name, and make weekly observations long.

```{r}
study_tidy_df =
  study_df |>
  mutate(files = str_replace(files, "\\.csv", "")) |>
  separate(files, into = c("arm", "subject_id"), sep = "_") |>
  mutate(
    arm = if_else(arm == "con", "Control", "Experimental"),
    subject_id = str_c(arm, "_", subject_id)
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    week_1:week_8,
    names_to = "week",
    values_to = "observation",
    names_prefix = "week_"
  ) |>
  mutate(week = as.numeric(week)) |>
  select(arm, subject_id, week, observation)

study_tidy_df
```

Make a spaghetti plot showing observations on each subject over time.

```{r}
study_tidy_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = week, y = observation, group = subject_id, color = arm)) +
  geom_point(alpha = .5) +
  geom_line(alpha = .7) +
  labs(
    title = "Observations over time for each subject",
    x = "Week",
    y = "Observation",
    color = "Arm"
  )
```

```{r include = FALSE}
arm_means =
  study_tidy_df |>
  filter(week %in% c(1, 8)) |>
  group_by(arm, week) |>
  summarize(mean_obs = mean(observation), .groups = "drop")

con_w1 = arm_means |> filter(arm == "Control", week == 1) |> pull(mean_obs)
con_w8 = arm_means |> filter(arm == "Control", week == 8) |> pull(mean_obs)
exp_w1 = arm_means |> filter(arm == "Experimental", week == 1) |> pull(mean_obs)
exp_w8 = arm_means |> filter(arm == "Experimental", week == 8) |> pull(mean_obs)
```

The two arms start at similar levels in week 1 
(mean `r round(con_w1, 2)` in control vs 
`r round(exp_w1, 2)` in experimental). 
Subjects in the control arm stay roughly flat over the 8 weeks 
(mean `r round(con_w8, 2)` at week 8), 
while subjects in the experimental arm increase over time in a roughly linear way (mean `r round(exp_w8, 2)` at week 8). 
Therefore, the experimental arm shows a clear upward trend that the control arm does not.


## Problem 3
Write a function that simulates one dataset and runs a one-sample t-test.

```{r}
sim_ttest = function(n_obs = 30, mu = 0, sigma = 5) {

  sim_data = tibble(
    x = rnorm(n = n_obs, mean = mu, sd = sigma)
  )

  t.test(pull(sim_data, x), mu = 0) |>
    broom::tidy() |>
    select(mu_hat = estimate, p_value = p.value)

}
```

Generate 5000 datasets for each true mean from 0 to 6.

```{r}
ttest_results_df =
  expand_grid(
    true_mu = 0:6,
    iter = 1:5000
  ) |>
  mutate(
    est_df = map(true_mu, \(m) sim_ttest(mu = m))
  ) |>
  unnest(est_df) |>
  mutate(reject = p_value < 0.05)
```

Plot the power of the test against the true mean.

```{r}
ttest_results_df |>
  group_by(true_mu) |>
  summarize(power = mean(reject)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = true_mu, y = power)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line() +
  labs(
    title = "Power of the one-sample t-test by true mean",
    x = "True mean (mu)",
    y = "Power (proportion of null rejected)"
  )
```

```{r include = FALSE}
power_df =
  ttest_results_df |>
  group_by(true_mu) |>
  summarize(power = mean(reject))

power_0 = power_df |> filter(true_mu == 0) |> pull(power)
power_1 = power_df |> filter(true_mu == 1) |> pull(power)
power_3 = power_df |> filter(true_mu == 3) |> pull(power)
power_6 = power_df |> filter(true_mu == 6) |> pull(power)
```

Power increases with effect size. When the true mean is 0, the null is rejected `r round(power_0 * 100, 1)`% of the time (close to alpha = 0.05). Power is only `r round(power_1 * 100, 1)`% when the true mean is 1, rises to `r round(power_3 * 100, 1)`% at 3, and reaches `r round(power_6 * 100, 1)`% at 6. Therefore, larger effect sizes are much more likely to be detected.

Plot the average estimate of mu_hat, in all samples and only in samples where the null was rejected.

```{r}
mu_hat_df =
  ttest_results_df |>
  group_by(true_mu) |>
  summarize(
    all_samples = mean(mu_hat),
    null_rejected = mean(mu_hat[reject])
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    all_samples:null_rejected,
    names_to = "sample",
    values_to = "avg_mu_hat"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    sample = if_else(sample == "all_samples", "All samples", "Null rejected only")
  )

mu_hat_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = true_mu, y = avg_mu_hat, color = sample)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line() +
  labs(
    title = "Average estimate of mu vs true mu",
    x = "True mean (mu)",
    y = "Average estimate of mu",
    color = ""
  )
```

```{r include = FALSE}
rej_1 = mu_hat_df |> filter(true_mu == 1, sample == "Null rejected only") |> pull(avg_mu_hat)
rej_2 = mu_hat_df |> filter(true_mu == 2, sample == "Null rejected only") |> pull(avg_mu_hat)
rej_6 = mu_hat_df |> filter(true_mu == 6, sample == "Null rejected only") |> pull(avg_mu_hat)
```

Across all samples, the average mu_hat is very close to the true mean, since the sample mean is unbiased. In samples where the null was rejected, the average mu_hat is too high when the effect size is small, and gets close to the truth for large effect sizes.

Therefore, the sample average of mu_hat across tests that reject the null is not equal to the true mean when power is low. With small effects, only samples that happen to have a large mu_hat reach significance, so selecting on p< 0.05 overestimates the effect. When power is close to 1, almost all samples are rejected, so this selection has little effect and the average is close to the truth.
